podcast.body: "Strange Fruit" was a landmark 1939 anti-lynching song that was banned in some places by racists who considered it too incendiary. Activists sent copies to Southern senators who refused to outlaw lynching. It created the template for anti-racism and civil rights protest songs that followed. "Strange Fruit, the 1939 anti-lynching song from Billy Holiday that was banned in some places by racists who considered it to be too incendiary."

podcast.body: Holiday's most famous performance, "Strange Fruit," a highly political and inflammatory song about lynching, was rejected by her label, Columbia, and her producer, John Hammond, due to its controversial nature. Due to Columbia's refusal, Billy Holiday turned to Milt Gabler, a politically left-leaning friend and founder of Commodore, who negotiated a special deal with Columbia to produce and release the song on his Commodore label. It sold over a million copies, became arguably the most important recording in music history, and was named "Song of the Century" by Time magazine in December 1999. "That recording sold over a million copies and became arguably the most important recording in music history."
